profile.name: Abisola Morohunfolu
profile.biography: I build across the interface and the systems behind it. My work spans accessibility products, practical tools, and projects that help me understand how things work.

notes.title: From setup to results.
notes.text: Assessment setup and performance review belong to the same workflow. At TestAssessify, I helped lead frontend work across both.

notes.title: Following the code.
notes.text: In CodeCanvas, I’m exploring how much context a static graph can give a reviewer, and where it needs to admit uncertainty.

projects.title: Equally.ai
projects.summary: Bringing AI into accessibility workflows so teams can turn website issues into practical recommendations.
projects.contribution: Helping teams understand accessibility issues, improve their websites, and keep access to the tools they need.

sections.title: From an issue to a next step

children.text: An accessibility report can tell a team what is wrong without making the next step clear. I worked on recommendations that give people a starting point for making a change.
This included suggestions for text, descriptions of images, and checks on alt text. Teams could review the suggestions while working through the issues on their websites.
I worked across the customer tools people use to review audits, manage websites, and act on findings. That also included Flowy, which brings accessibility checks into the browser.
Smaller tasks mattered too: reusing website settings, finding and exporting records, and reaching billing information and invoices.

sections.title: Keep access in step with a renewal

children.text: When a customer renews, their website access should reflect it. I helped address cases where the product still showed an older expiration date after a renewal.
The goal was to keep the customer’s subscription and access aligned so they could continue using the product.
The useful part of an AI suggestion is what someone can do with it. I learned to think about where a recommendation appears, what it needs to explain, and how it helps a person move forward.
Working across these parts of the product helped me see the customer’s task as a whole.

cover.alt: Equally.ai website introducing its web accessibility products
cover.caption: Equally.ai’s public website.

projects.collaborators: Built with the Equally.ai engineering team. I contributed the AWS Bedrock integration and recommendation tools, alongside shared work on the AI workflow, customer interfaces, and supporting services.
introduction: Equally.ai: bringing AI into accessibility work.
I helped bring AI recommendations into the way teams find and fix accessibility issues on their websites.
Someone reviewing an issue could get suggestions for what to change, including image descriptions and alt text, and decide how to use them.
I also worked on the wider customer experience, from reviewing website issues to managing subscriptions and access.
impactEvidence: Teams can review suggested changes alongside accessibility findings.
Image descriptions and alt-text checks help people review website images.
Customers can manage website access, subscriptions, and billing through the product.

projects.title: Flowy
projects.summary: Accessibility audits where you work: inspect a website and review issues from the browser.
projects.contribution: Check a website for accessibility issues and review what needs attention without leaving the browser.

sections.title: Check the page you are working on

children.text: Flowy lets people review accessibility issues while browsing a website. I worked on the experience for finding issues and understanding what needs attention as part of the Equally.ai team.
It brings the audit closer to the page itself, so a developer or content editor can move between a finding and the work of addressing it.

cover.alt: Flowy website introducing its browser-based accessibility audit tool
cover.caption: Flowy’s website.

projects.collaborators: Built with the Equally.ai team. Flowy is part of the wider platform, with shared audit and recommendation systems.

projects.title: Room Planner
projects.summary: See how a room fits before moving furniture. Compare layouts, edit dimensions, and take a plan with you.
projects.contribution: Plan a room, try furniture arrangements, compare alternatives, and share the result before moving anything.

gallery.alt: Room Planner floor plan with measured furniture and room controls
gallery.caption: The same room as a measured floor plan.

gallery.alt: Room Planner shared room view on a mobile screen
gallery.caption: The room shared on a phone.

sections.title: Try the room before moving anything

children.text: Change room dimensions, position furniture, and try different finishes. The floor plan helps with measurements; the 3D view makes the arrangement easier to picture.
Fit notes flag furniture overlaps, gaps, and door swings so there is more to go on than how the layout looks.
I wanted it to be easy to try a second idea without undoing the first. Save separate alternatives and compare arrangements without overwriting the version you started with.
Take the plan with you as a measured PDF, a floor-plan image, a furniture list, or a file you can open again.
Send someone a view of the room that they can inspect or save as their own copy. The version you shared stays the same while you continue working on your original.
Shared links last for 30 days, and you can revoke a link when it is no longer needed.

cover.alt: Room Planner showing a furnished living room in 3D beside finish controls
cover.caption: A real room in the planner, with editable wall and furniture finishes.

introduction: Room Planner
I built Room Planner to make it easier to work out whether a room layout will fit before moving furniture.
Draw the room, add furniture, and switch between a floor plan and a 3D view. Try another arrangement without losing the first one, then save or share the plan.

projects.title: System Playground
projects.summary: Make runtime behavior visible. Follow requests through the event loop, queues, and worker pool.
projects.contribution: See how requests move through a program, what waits in a queue, and what happens next.

children.text: Reading about the event loop is one thing; seeing a request wait, run, and hand work off makes the sequence easier to understand.
I started with Node.js as a way to explore these ideas visually. The playground is a place to experiment with runtime behavior and build a clearer picture of what is happening.

cover.alt: System Playground showing event loop phases, queues and worker activity
cover.caption: Following requests through the Node.js event loop.

introduction: System Playground
I built System Playground to make the parts of a program that are usually invisible easier to follow.
The Node.js playground lets you watch requests move between the call stack, queues, and workers. It is a model for exploring how things work, with the sequence laid out in front of you.

projects.title: TestAssessify
projects.summary: Helping hiring teams set up assessments and track candidate performance in one place.
projects.contribution: Prepare candidate assessments and bring the results together so hiring teams can decide whom to progress.

children.text: TestAssessify helps hiring teams assess candidates against the requirements of a role. The platform supports choosing assessments from a library or creating custom assessments.
I helped lead the frontend work for assessment setup: the experience hiring teams use to prepare the tests candidates will take.
Once candidates take an assessment, the results need to support a hiring decision. I helped lead frontend development for the admin dashboard used to track candidate performance.
The dashboard brought performance information into the team’s review workflow, helping administrators understand how candidates performed and use those results when deciding whom to progress.

cover.alt: Current TestAssessify homepage introducing its recruitment assessment platform, with hiring information beside two professionals
cover.caption: TestAssessify’s homepage.

projects.collaborators: Built with the team at my previous employer.
introduction: TestAssessify: from assessments to hiring insight.
Hiring teams need more than a test. They need a way to set up assessments and understand what the results say about each candidate.

At my previous employer, I helped lead frontend development for TestAssessify’s assessment setup and admin dashboard. My work connected preparing an assessment with tracking candidate performance, supporting the team’s decisions throughout the hiring process.
impactEvidence: Hiring teams can prepare assessments within the product.
Administrators can track candidate performance through the dashboard.
Assessment results inform which candidates move forward in the hiring process.

projects.title: CodeCanvas
projects.summary: Find your way through a codebase and understand a change before reviewing it.
projects.contribution: Explore how parts of a codebase connect, follow a path through the code, and review a change with its surrounding context.

sections.title: Find a way into the code

children.text: Start with the map to see how the parts connect, then narrow in on a route or a function. Guided paths help explain how one part leads to another.
The map comes from reading the source code. Where a connection is uncertain, CodeCanvas makes that uncertainty visible.
A diff shows the lines that changed. I wanted a view of the surrounding code too: where a changed function is used, which entry points lead to it, and what else may need a closer look.
CodeCanvas keeps that exploration alongside the review, so it is easier to ask useful questions about a change.

introduction: CodeCanvas
I built CodeCanvas to help me find my way through a codebase without holding the whole thing in my head.
It turns relationships in TypeScript code into a map I can explore, then helps me follow a path or see where a change might reach.

projects.title: Monieplans
projects.summary: Give money a purpose, log transactions, and compare the plan with what actually happened.
projects.contribution: Give your money a monthly plan, keep everyday spending manageable, and adjust when your priorities change.

gallery.alt: Monieplans budget category showing available funds, original target, current allocation, and recent expenses
gallery.caption: A budget category with available funds, allocations, and recent expenses.

gallery.alt: Monieplans mobile monthly review with sample spending totals, category breakdowns, and weekly allocations
gallery.caption: Monthly spending, category totals, and weekly allocations on mobile.

sections.title: Make the month easier to manage

children.text: I wanted a plan that distinguishes fixed needs from everyday spending. Rent or fuel can stay monthly, while groceries and other flexible categories can be paced week by week.
Log expenses as they happen and see what is still available. The aim is to make the next spending decision easier to understand.

sections.title: Leave room for a change of plan

children.text: A budget should be useful when things change too. Move unused money to the category that needs it, while keeping the original target visible.
The monthly review brings spending and adjustments together, so you can see what happened and use it when planning the next month.

cover.alt: Monieplans homepage introducing flexible monthly budgets and showing how money moves between categories
cover.caption: Monieplans’ homepage.

introduction: Monieplans
Monieplans is my take on a budget that can bend with real life.

Set a monthly spending limit, give each category a purpose, and pace everyday spending through the weeks. When plans change, move unused money between categories while keeping your original targets in view.

projects.title: Moodboard
projects.summary: Collect images, notes, and links on a board you can arrange and share.
projects.contribution: Bring images, notes, and links together, arrange ideas your way, and share a board with someone else.

gallery.alt: Moodboard editor with a saved note, image, and reference link arranged on the canvas
gallery.caption: Images, notes, and links arranged on a Moodboard canvas.

children.text: Put images, links, and notes beside one another, then move them around as the idea takes shape. Sections help group references without forcing every board into the same structure.
I wanted collecting something to be a small action: paste a link, drop in an image, or write a note and keep going.
Share a board so someone else can see the references together. For client work, feedback and approvals can sit alongside the ideas being discussed.
The aim is to make it easier to talk about a direction when everyone can see what it looks like.

cover.alt: Moodboard landing page showing a sample board of room photographs, material references, and notes
cover.caption: Moodboard’s homepage.

introduction: Moodboard
I’m building Moodboard as a place for ideas that would otherwise end up scattered across tabs, screenshots, and notes.
Save images, add a thought, or keep a link on a board you can arrange your way. Use it for a room, a creative project, or whatever you are thinking through.

projects.title: Shortty
projects.summary: A small URL-shortening interface with a simple copy-and-share flow.
projects.contribution: Turn a long link into a shorter one that is easy to copy and share.

children.text: I kept the interaction focused on the link: one place to paste it, a clear result, and an easy way to copy it.
It was a chance to work through a compact product experience, from entering a URL to sharing the result.

introduction: Shortty
Shortty is an earlier personal project built around a small, everyday task: making a long link easier to share.
Paste a URL, get a shorter link, and copy it without extra steps.
